en: Kanchoro ran up
And took his White Falcon.
Your dear mother Kanykey
Had fashioned an ornate golden perch;
He set the White Falcon upon it
And bound it securely again.
The pampered wife Chachykey,
Her silk with gathered folds,
Her flowing silk rustling,
Stepped backward, hanging back,
Acting coyly like a young child.
Semetey came toward the encampment,
Leading Chachykey by the hand.
He brought her inside with affection,
And set aflame every unburning place
Within Chürök, who watched them:
“His unbearably pampered wife
Struts about, the infidel!
I shall find the right way to speak with her;
If the woman comes to terms,
I shall accept her as an elder sister.
If the woman will not come to terms,
I shall settle our account together;
I shall take her husband away
And cast her into suffering!”
The wretched woman had studied Arabic
And become expert in the language.
When the sun quivered toward setting,
When the people were preparing to sleep,
When the livestock had been tethered,
And the people's arrangements were complete,
Twilight entered and deepened;
Stars of every kind crowded the sky.
Without appearing before a single person,
Without being noticed by anyone,
The pampered wife Chachykey
Went to have a private talk.
If the woman agreed to reason,
She would become her companion;
If the woman would not listen,
She would bring about her utter ruin.
If Chachykey found the proper way,
She would take her as an elder sister,
Serve beneath her,
And, if the poor woman came to her senses,
Stand before her with many entreaties,
Her knees bent to the ground,
Bowing her head in submission.
A sheer cliff rises in the valley;
The wretched daughter of Akun,
An old bondwoman who had seen much,
A sharp bondwoman skilled in transformation,
Stretched herself like a lynx.
Reluctant to spend words in speaking,
She moved obliquely like a white doe.
The unfortunate daughter of Akun
Set aside her pride and began to speak.
On the bank of broad Keng-Kol,
Where twin plane trees had grown,
Aychürök lay in wait
At the place where the pampered wife
Would go to relieve herself.
At Chachykey's side were forty
Attendant daughters-in-law:
Twenty married women and twenty girls,
Drawn from the Argyn and the Kyrgyz.
Weeping wildly in extreme distress,
She had devoted those forty
To accompany her at her side.
Broad-rumped, with long hair ornaments,
The young married women were beautiful;
In red dresses, with reed-slender waists,
The girls were exceedingly beautiful.
The pampered wife Chachykey
Prepared herself with eager resolve;
Such was her stately appearance,
Swaying as though struck by a hero.
Twenty were on her right,
Her companions sharing one life,
Coming out while supporting her;
Twenty were on her left,
Her companions who would share her suffering,
And they too came supporting her.
Wrapped entirely in silk,
Holding a white silk kerchief,
Turning without stepping firmly,
Composing herself like a noblewoman,
Showing a flank like an argali,
Displaying her white breast,
When your mother came before her,
Aychürök, daughter of Akun,
Turned obliquely like a parrot
And now began speaking
To the pampered, ill-tempered wife.
Speaking softly but striking hard,
Each of her words bit deeply:
“Elder sister, listen to my circumstances!
I fell in love with your husband and suffer;
I plead with you, calling you elder sister.
This dear hair grown down my back—
Setting aside my pride and wandering,
I have come before you, poor soul.
I shall make you a gift of livestock;
Take my red-tailed elephant,
My precious elder sister, heed my words.
Bowing before your face,
I bent my knee and lowered my head.
If you are human, you will understand
And consent to these words of mine.
My words are gold; understand them,
My caravan, my sister, heed my words!
The people are a treasury, a great river;
Though poured out by the bucket, they do not end.
Your gray wolf is a deep-rooted treasure.
Red silk and fine fabric,
Precious garments and mail—
What if we both wore them, sister?
What if we became elder and younger sisters
And married the same man, sister?
What if we joined in celebration and kept a home
And lived together, sister?
If he lies with you for six days,
Let him lie with me on the remaining day;
Let him lie with you seven days,
And with me on the day that does not fit.
I shall hear your stern words;
I shall enter with your fire
And leave with your ashes.
I shall bow my neck to you
And perform your service.
I have spoken wise words; understand them;
Do not make me wail—heed me, sister!
If you heed my words, elder sister,
I am the fortune granted to you;
If you do not heed them, elder sister,
I am the wrinkle upon your brow!
I am the blessed night that met you;
If my conduct pleases you, sister,
I shall be one of your servants.
Searching the whole world,
I have come here deliberately
After roaming among all its peoples.
I have come to braid
The side-locks beside my cheeks, sister;
I have come to serve you
And surrender myself before you, sister!
Understand these words of mine;
My precious sister, heed my words!
Listen to this reasoning of mine:
I came searching from Afghanistan
For the husband destined to me long ago!”
After Chürök had spoken thus,
At that moment Chachykey
Prepared herself with shrill resolve,
Swaying as though struck by a hero.
She spoke harshly, snarling,
And assailed Chürök to her face:
“An old maid like you, who never took a husband,
Has caused trouble many times;
A sharp-tongued woman like you from ancient days!
There is no place you have not worshiped,
No man you have not wandered after;
Do not grow excited without cause!
In the city of Khan Akun
You wandered long in yearning.
Hearing you called shameless,
Your gray-wolf husband took offense.
In the place of his father, Khan Akun,
His words filled with venom,
You sat until you grew old.
Spit, spit upon your face, woman!
I will not consent to what you say;
I will not surrender Ayköl alive.
Do not take him from my hands without right.
The bloodthirsty, unfortunate lord
Has no father-in-law named Khan Akun,
And no wife named Aychürök!
Listen, woman, to my words;
I shall cool your ardor!
I will not agree to these words of yours.
Before your husband does so,
I shall give you a letter of divorce.
Gird your roaming waist,
Wander and find for yourself
The husband you are to marry!
I will not agree to what you say;
While my dear life remains,
I will not give away my bloodthirsty one!
Upon your girded waist,
Go away without shrieking
To the husband you have been seeking!
A steep cliff rises by the running spring;
Do not wail, wretched woman!
You are the eye of one who travels by night;
Your appearance seems cold,
You are the very devil and demon!
At the words you speak,
I stand amazed at you.
You appeared like an albasty
Before these eyes of mine.
I am Semetey's wife;
Keep away and do not approach.
Do not cast sorcery, woman.
Minced about here and there,
You appear to have the ways of a mare;
When I test you from every side,
You appear to have the ways of Satan!
Are you an evil spirit risen from the water,
Or a sly creature roaming to lead men astray?”
Speaking cold words,
The pampered wife Chachykey—
God now struck the foolish woman—
Spoke words colder than all:
“I shall bind up the hair down my back;
If I let my lord be taken,
May I marry my father Shaatemir!”
Humiliated, crying aloud,
Unable to find her bearings,
Aychürök, daughter of Akun,
Now wept with heaving sobs.
Her heart broke apart,
And tears poured from her eyes:
“Alas, sister, may you come to no good!
We already knew your rudeness—
Your father-in-law who passed to the other world,
